title: Evaluate the affect that various factors have on the viability of perishable produce exportation

lessons.title: Global factors and market requirement variances
lessons.html:
The impact of global factors on South African exports

The viability of exporting a product is the question of whether, after all costs and risks, it earns a better return than selling locally or not producing at all. A manager must evaluate global factors, not just list them.

  • Counter-seasonality: South Africa's Southern Hemisphere timing creates windows into Europe, the UK and North America. The value of the window depends on how much competing supply arrives from Chile, Peru, Argentina, Australia, New Zealand and Northern Hemisphere storage. For example, late-season South African apples compete with Northern Hemisphere fruit coming out of CA storage.
  • Trade agreements and tariffs: preferential access lowers costs compared with competitors who pay full duties. Losing such access, or a competitor gaining it, shifts relative profitability.
  • Global economic conditions: recession in a major market lowers demand for premium fruit and pushes buyers to cheaper classes or origins.
  • Logistics disruptions: global container shortages, canal closures or rerouting raise freight costs and transit times, which hits low-value or short-shelf-life products hardest.
  • Sustainability and ethical demands: requirements for social compliance, water stewardship and carbon footprint add costs but are increasingly a condition for supplying major retailers.

Variances between SA standards and market requirements

South African export standards set minimum requirements. Individual markets and buyers often differ:

AreaTypical varianceImplication
ResiduesLower MRLs, or limits on the number of activesSpray programmes must be designed per market
PhytosanitarySpecific pest protocols, cold treatmentExtra cost, longer transit, registration a season ahead
Quality specsStricter size, colour or BrixHigher packout loss; lower volumes qualify
PackagingRetail-ready packs, labels, recyclable materialsHigher packing cost and complexity

Each variance changes the cost per carton and the share of the crop that qualifies, so it must be built into the viability calculation for each market.

lessons.title: Market forces and external factors in viability decisions
lessons.html:
Market forces and their effects

  • Supply and demand: oversupply in a market week drives prices down sharply for perishable products, because fruit cannot be held back for long. Exporters use programmes with retailers, market diversification and staggered shipping to reduce the risk.
  • Buyer concentration: a few large retailers control much of the trade in some markets. This brings stable programmes but also price pressure and the risk of losing a programme.
  • Exchange rate: most exports are priced in foreign currency while most costs are in rand. A weaker rand improves rand returns; a stronger rand squeezes margins. Exporters may use forward cover to manage this risk.
  • Competition between suppliers: competitors with lower costs, shorter shipping distances or newer cultivars can capture shelf space.
  • Cultivar and brand rights: licensed cultivars and brands can earn premiums but involve royalties and marketing conditions.

External factors and their effects

  • Climate: drought, hail and heat waves reduce volumes and packouts; climate trends may shift which regions suit which crops.
  • Pests and diseases: a pest detection in a market can close it or require extra treatments.
  • Infrastructure: port congestion, unreliable electricity and rail problems raise costs and risk of cold chain breaks.
  • Input costs: fuel, electricity, packaging, fertiliser and labour increase faster than prices in some years.
  • Policy: changes in labour law, land, water allocation and trade policy affect investment decisions.

Evaluating viability

A simple evaluation compares, for each market option, the expected net return per carton (price in rand minus freight, commissions, levies, packing and treatments) multiplied by the volume that will qualify, against the local market alternative. Then test the result under different scenarios: a weaker or stronger rand, a 20 percent lower price, longer transit, or a market closure. A market that only works in the best case is high risk.

Example: a grower considers a distant Asian market for plums. The price is higher, but cold treatment, longer transit, higher rejection risk and freight cut the net return. After scenario testing, the grower sends only the best-storing cultivars there and keeps the rest for nearer markets.

Key points

  • Viability means net return after costs and risks, compared with alternatives.
  • Market requirements often vary from SA minimum standards and add cost.
  • Supply, buyer power and exchange rates strongly affect returns.
  • Climate, pests, infrastructure and input costs are major external risks.
  • Test decisions with scenarios, not only the best case.
